A1-A2.headline: The History and Politics Behind Greater Albania

pages.text: Greater Albania is a nationalist political idea seeking to unite regions where ethnic Albanians live into one shared homeland. The concept grew from the nineteenth-century League of Prizren, which proposed grouping autonomous Albanian lands inside the Ottoman Empire.
pages.caption: Proposal of 4 autonomous "Albanian vilayets" within the Ottoman Empire by the League of Prizren, as agreed after the Albanian revolt of 1912

evidence.articleCaption: Proposal of 4 autonomous "Albanian vilayets" within the Ottoman Empire by the League of Prizren, as agreed after the Albanian revolt of 1912

pages.text: Many Albanian nationalists actually dislike the phrase Greater Albania and prefer calling the same concept Ethnic Albania instead. In Albanian speech, Ethnic Albania describes territories they view as their traditional historic homeland across neighboring Balkan borders.

During World War Two, Italian leader Benito Mussolini invaded Albania and established an Italian protectorate over Albanian lands. Fascist leaders promoted Albanian irredentism to win local backing, while deep tensions broke out across Kosovo between Albanians and Serbian settlers.
pages.caption: The Italian Protectorate of Albania established by Italy in August 1941.

evidence.articleCaption: The Italian Protectorate of Albania established by Italy in August 1941.

pages.text: In the twenty-first century, nationalist political parties in Albania still formed around supporting a Greater Albania across the Balkans. Even pop culture sparked sharp regional debate when singer Dua Lipa faced backlash for sharing a nationalist banner previously seen at a Serbia versus Albania football match.

From the League of Prizren under Ottoman rule through wartime occupation and modern Balkan politics, the idea of Greater Albania has remained sensitive. Competing memories of borders, identity, and regional peace continue shaping debates among Albanians and their neighbors.

title: How Lhasa Newar Merchants Bridged Nepal and Tibet

A1-A2.headline: Lhasa Newar: Traders and Artists Across the Himalaya

pages.text: Lhasa Newar were skilled Nepalese traders and Buddhist artisans who traveled for centuries between the Kathmandu Valley and Tibet. Guiding caravans across high mountain passes in Tibet, these merchants bridged Nepal, Tibet, and eastern India while spreading Himalayan art.
pages.caption: A caravan crossing the Tuna Plain in Tibet, Mt. Chomolhari in background.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bundesarchiv Bild 135-S-10-04-32, Tibetexpedition, Karawane vor Chomolhari.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A caravan crossing the Tuna Plain in Tibet, Mt. Chomolhari in background.

pages.text: Newar traders carried metal utensils, sacred statues, and rice from Nepal alongside textiles and factory goods from India northward into Tibet. Strong mule, donkey, and yak caravans hauled heavy packs over the Tibetan Plateau while mountain porters crossed Nepal's steep trails.

Alongside business houses, gifted Lhasa Newar artisans shaped sacred Buddhist art across Tibet and Central Asia. They sculpted statues, painted frescoes and stupas, and crafted gleaming gilt roofs for major landmarks like Lhasa's Jokhang Temple.

This thousand-year Lhasa Newar commercial tradition ended abruptly when war between India and China closed the vital caravan corridor through Sikkim. Cut off from their historic mountain route, Nepalese merchants and craftsmen closed their Tibetan shops and returned home.

Even after modern border closures ended the caravan era, gleaming roofs, painted temples, and shared cultural memories still preserve the Lhasa Newar legacy. For a millennium, their fearless mountain journeys united Himalayan economies and artistic traditions closely.

B1-B2.headline: How Lhasa Newar Merchants Bridged Nepal and Tibet

pages.text: For centuries, the expatriate Lhasa Newar community of Nepalese merchants and artisans traveled regularly between the Kathmandu Valley and Tibet. Running long-distance mountain caravans across Tibet and Bengal, they simultaneously fueled Himalayan commerce and cross-border Buddhist artistic exchange.
pages.caption: A caravan crossing the Tuna Plain in Tibet, Mt. Chomolhari in background.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bundesarchiv Bild 135-S-10-04-32, Tibetexpedition, Karawane vor Chomolhari.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A caravan crossing the Tuna Plain in Tibet, Mt. Chomolhari in background.

pages.text: Newar trading houses exported Nepalese metal utensils, sacred statues, and rice along with Indian textiles and manufactured goods into Tibet, returning with Central Asian products. Porters shouldered cargo across Nepal's rugged slopes before mule, donkey, and yak caravans crossed the Tibetan Plateau.

Equally renowned for sacred craftsmanship, Lhasa Newar artisans sculpted statues, painted paubhas and temple murals, and shaped Buddhist architecture across Tibet. French traveler Évariste Régis Huc marveled at how prized Newar craftsmen constructed gleaming gilt roofs on revered Tibetan shrines.

This remarkable thousand-year commercial network came to an abrupt close when the Sino-Indian War shut down the crucial Sikkim caravan highway linking India and Tibet. Unable to sustain overland business, expatriate merchants and artists shuttered their Lhasa shops and returned to Nepal.

Though twentieth-century geopolitics closed their historic trade roads, the Lhasa Newar imprint remains vividly visible across Himalayan temples and crafts. Their blend of daring mountain enterprise and artistic mastery stands among Asia's most memorable cultural bridges.

A1-A2.headline: Why Britain Ended Wild Badger Culling

pages.text: Badger culling in the United Kingdom tried to cut wild badger numbers to stop cattle illness. Officials hoped fewer European badgers would halt bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis bacteria. Milk pasteurisation and human vaccines already keep risk to people very low.
pages.caption: Badger protesting outside the Home Office.

evidence.articleCaption: Badger protesting outside the Home Office.

pages.text: After years of debate, officials stopped issuing fresh licenses and turned toward wildlife vaccination instead. Earlier trials in Wales ended when leaders decided culling failed to work well. Later English pilot zones tested free shooting methods before new rules phased culling out.

European badgers are not endangered, yet strict British laws protect these quiet wild animals. Years ago, workers gassed underground badger setts while trying to fight rabies across Europe. Compulsory cattle testing and herd checks gradually reshaped national farm policy.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text: Independent scientists led an influential national review requesting careful field experiments on badger culling. Follow-up studies later tracked cattle infections after local badger operations stopped. Researchers found temporary benefits inside culled zones disappeared completely within three quiet years.

Though cattle face the heaviest harm, Mycobacterium bovis bacteria can also infect human patients. Older British patients occasionally contracted infection decades ago before milk pasteurisation spread everywhere. Today safer vaccines and clean dairy practices shield both rural herds and families.

B1-B2.headline: Science and Politics Around UK Badger Culling

pages.text: Badger culling in the United Kingdom sought to curb bovine tuberculosis by shrinking wild badger populations. Caused by Mycobacterium bovis bacteria, the infection harms cattle herds heavily while threatening occasional human cases. Public safeguards like pasteurisation and vaccination keep human risk minimal.

pages.text: Policy shifted decisively away from shooting licenses toward vaccination to block disease spread naturally. Welsh authorities cancelled targeted culling early after concluding field results proved ineffective. Subsequent English trials sparked intense protests outside government offices over humaneness and scientific value.

Though abundant across British woodlands, wild badgers enjoy extensive legal protection under national wildlife statutes. Decades earlier, authorities across Europe gassed underground badger setts hoping to contain rabies. Mandatory herd tests eventually modernized rural cattle disease control.

pages.text: Scientific uncertainty led the Krebs Report to demand rigorous randomised culling trials across Britain. Later follow-up studies revealed modest infection reductions inside culled areas faded entirely within a few years. Temporary disruption also complicated disease patterns along neighboring farmland edges.

Occasionally, the Mycobacterium bovis bacterium still causes zoonotic illness among British patients. Most reported human infections occurred in older citizens exposed before pasteurised milk became universal. Expanding wildlife vaccination offers a calmer path balancing farming and animal welfare.

C1-C2.headline: Evaluating Evidence Behind British Badger Culling Policy

pages.text: Authorized across parts of Britain, badger culling attempted to suppress bovine tuberculosis by reducing wildlife reservoirs. Driven by Mycobacterium bovis transmission between European badgers and cattle, the controversy pitted farmers against conservationists. Routine milk pasteurisation and vaccines shielded humans effectively.

pages.text: Recent UK policy pivoted firmly away from granting fresh badger culling licences toward badger vaccination. Earlier Welsh administrations halted targeted operations after concluding culling lacked efficacy, whereas English pilots scrutinized shooting humaneness. Persistent public demonstrations urged lasting statutory protection.

Legally sheltered under protective British statutes, wild badgers paradoxically faced periodic control campaigns over decades. Cold-war European teams even gassed underground badger setts amid rabies scares before mandatory bovine testing expanded. Shifting veterinary strategies continually reshaped wildlife management.

Subsequent follow-up monitoring demonstrated initial cattle reductions vanished entirely within three post-cull years. Border zones showed equally fleeting effects, undermining arguments for lethal intervention.

Documented human infections with Mycobacterium bovis largely reflect historical exposures predating universal milk pasteurisation. Moving permanently from contested badger culling toward vaccination aligns veterinary control with ecological conservation. Evidence-driven policy gradually resolves decades of heated rural conflict.

A1-A2.headline: Aden: Yemen's Ancient Port by the Red Sea

pages.text: Aden is an ancient Yemeni port city resting cleanly on rocky volcanic hills beside calm blue seas. Sitting near the eastern mouth of the Red Sea, the Port of Aden connects Asia, Africa, and Europe. Today Aden stands among Yemen's biggest coastal cities.
pages.caption: Port of Aden from the ISS, 2016

pages.text: In ancient Arabic speech, the name Aden means peaceful settlement and steady welcoming home for weary ships. Greek merchants called this thriving harbor Arabia Emporion along rich sea trade routes linking India and Europe. Tall volcanic cliffs protected quiet anchored boats cleanly.

Early local kingdoms built modest defensive walls here before Islamic centuries reshaped regional trade slowly. During early Islamic dynasties, Aden waited through quiet years until bold rebuilding changed its rocky harbor forever. Strong stone towers soon overlooked calm sunlit waters.

Major solid rebuilding later turned Aden into a bustling sea hub welcoming merchants from Egypt, India, and China. Sailors swapped spices, cloth, and fine crafts while diverse travelers settled along busy waterfront alleys. Medieval geographers marveled at busy docks packed with international vessels.

Across centuries, kingdoms, traders, and empires valued Aden's bright natural shelter between Indian and Red Sea lanes. Today millions of Yemeni citizens live around the historic harbor towns stretching cleanly across volcanic headlands. Aden remains a proud gateway between continents.

B1-B2.headline: Crossroads of Trade: The Historic Port of Aden

pages.text: Positioned along Arabia's southern tip near the Red Sea entrance, Aden remains one of Yemen's most historic harbors. Encompassing eight coastal districts, the sprawling Port of Aden serves today as Yemen's temporary administrative seat. Volcanic crater walls still shelter deep waterfront anchorages.

pages.text: Arabic geographers celebrated the name Aden as meaning residence and safe home for visiting sailing ships. Classical Greek merchants christened it Arabia Emporion because favorable monsoon winds guided commerce directly between India and Egypt. Natural volcanic bays offered matchless coastal protection.

While early Yemeni Himyar rulers raised monumental forts inland, Aden initially required comparatively modest coastal walls. After Islam arrived, regional trade stalled briefly across early Islamic dynasties until dynamic medieval commerce revived. Fortified watchtowers eventually guarded strategic bay ridges.

Ambitious medieval reconstruction transformed Aden into an international marketplace drawing sailors from East Africa, Sindh, and China. Geographer Muqaddasi noted bustling multicultural neighborhoods where Persian merchants thrived beside local Arab traders. Warehouses overflowed with frankincense, textiles, and eastern spices.

From ancient Arabian peninsula roots toward modern cities in Yemen, Aden's historic harbor attracted sailors and merchants continuously. Today its estimated population anchors coastal districts serving as the recognized administrative capital across the Gulf of Aden. Ancient maritime trade legacies remain vibrant.

C1-C2.headline: Maritime Continuity and Crossroads Heritage of Aden

pages.text: Commanding Arabia's southwestern coast beside the Bab el-Mandeb approach, Aden endures as a premier Indian Ocean harbor. Sprawling across eight districts, the storied Port of Aden functions today as Yemen's internationally recognized administrative center. Dramatic extinct volcanic peaks cradle deep natural anchorages.

pages.text: Etymologically evoking settlement and safe anchorage for ships, Aden earned classical acclaim as Greek merchants' Arabia Emporion. Positioned ideally along maritime corridors linking Indian spice ports toward Mediterranean markets, its sheltered harbor proved irresistibly strategic. Towering basalt cliffs buffered seasonal winds.

Although pre-Islamic Himyarite kingdoms erected impressive inland citadels elsewhere, early coastal fortification around Aden remained modest. Following Islam's arrival and quiet early centuries under provincial governors, renewed stability catalyzed ambitious civic expansion. Durable stone masonry eventually ringed key port ridges.

Comprehensive medieval reconstruction reestablished Aden as a cosmopolitan entrepôt uniting merchants from Gujarat, Egypt, East Africa, and China. Chronicler Muqaddasi vividly documented diverse quarters thriving on vibrant transoceanic exchange. Wealthy merchant houses transformed rugged crater shores into legendary trading neighborhoods.

Across empires spanning Himyarite antiquity, medieval sultanates, and contemporary Yemen, geographic destiny perpetually defined the Port of Aden. Home to over a million citizens, the historic city bridges Arabian shores seamlessly with global commerce. Centuries of seafaring resilience endure vibrantly today.

A1-A2.headline: Assisted Migration: Helping Wildlife Move as Climate Shifts

pages.text: Assisted migration is the deliberate relocation of plant or animal populations beyond their historic range so they can reach suitable habitats as climate changes. Conservation biologists introduced this form of species translocation to protect biodiversity from rapid warming.
pages.caption: Three types of assisted migration; assisted population migration (left), assisted range migration (center) and assisted species migration (right)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Assisted migration 3 types 2022 (cropped).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Three types of assisted migration; assisted population migration (left), assisted range migration (center) and assisted species migration (right)

pages.text: Forestry scientists and conservation biologists often discuss assisted migration from different perspectives in their own journals. Foresters pay special attention because ancient ecological records show some tree species spread too slowly on their own during past climate shifts.

One well-known American example involves the critically endangered Florida torreya, a rare yew-family tree native to the border of northern Florida and southwestern Georgia. Dedicated volunteers known as the Torreya Guardians have carefully sent donated seeds to cooler northern planting sites.

Conservation efforts have also studied insects such as the Quino checkerspot butterfly, a threatened native subspecies of southern California and northwestern Baja California. Closely related to Edith's checkerspot, this delicate butterfly highlights how shifting habitats challenge small wildlife.

Near Mexico City, a combined assisted migration project planted high-altitude trees favored by overwintering Monarch butterflies, while ordinary gardeners planting native trees further north have already started inadvertent migration. Together, these efforts test how humans can help ecosystems adapt safely.

pages.text: Assisted migration refers to intentionally establishing wildlife or plant populations beyond a species' historic range so they can track suitable habitats amid changing climate. pages.text: Forestry science and conservation biology approach assisted migration through distinct journals and priorities. Paleoecological evidence showing that tree ranges often lagged behind prehistoric climate shifts has long persuaded forestry managers to evaluate proactive seed movement.

In the southeastern United States, the critically endangered Florida torreya tree survives narrowly along the northern Florida and southwestern Georgia border. A self-organized citizen group called the Torreya Guardians has championed moving donated seeds northward into cooler habitats.

Insect conservation likewise spotlights the Quino checkerspot butterfly, a vulnerable subspecies native to southern California and northwestern Baja California. Belonging to the broader Edith's checkerspot lineage stretching to British Columbia, the butterfly underscores localized climate vulnerability.

Encouraging results recently emerged from a coupled plant-and-animal assisted migration trial near Mexico City planting high-altitude oyamel trees for overwintering Monarch butterflies. Meanwhile, mature horticultural trees planted north of native boundaries reveal inadvertent assisted migration already underway.

pages.text: Assisted migration denotes the intentional establishment of populations or meta-populations beyond a species' historic range to track viable habitats through accelerating climate change. A1-A2.headline: Folklore of the European Changeling Myth

pages.text: A changeling is a mysterious creature found across old European legends and folk stories. Storytellers claimed fairies, trolls, or elves secretly swapped a human baby for one of their own. Families told these tales when an infant suddenly seemed strange or sickly.
pages.caption: Devil swapping a child in crib with changeling called Killecroff ―Illustrated by Gustav Doré, Saintine (1862) Mythologie du Rhin

pages.text: In Irish tales, a changeling looked weak, stopped growing, and spoke with sharp uncanny wisdom. People watched whether the strange baby danced joyfully whenever left completely alone in the room. Parents sometimes hung iron scissors or reversed coats hoping to guard babies.

Folklorists explain that changeling stories reflected painful hunger among poor peasant farming families. Feeding a child who could not work stretched scarce village food supplies very thin. Myth gave struggling communities a way to express unspoken grief and hardship.

In Scandinavian folklore, families believed trolls admired human manners and wanted human upbringings for babies. Parents placed iron knives or scissors above cradles to frighten away underground trolls safely. Bright blond hair and blue eyes supposedly drew fairy curiosity too.

One warm Swedish story praised a gentle mother who refused to harm a troll baby left with her. Because she treated the helpless changeling kindly, her real son returned safely from the forest. Author Helena Nyblom later retold this memorable Nordic fairy tale.

Across European folklore, a changeling was a supernatural substitute allegedly left behind when spirits stole a child. Legends blamed fairies, elves, trolls, and demons for taking human infants from unguarded cradles. Occasionally, tales even imagined aged spirits trading places to enjoy gentle care.

pages.text: Traditional Irish legends described changelings as pale, frail children displaying adult teeth, beards, or unsettling wit. Observers believed a hidden fairy betrayed itself by dancing energetically once nobody seemed to watch. Simple protective charms relied upon iron scissors or inverted coats.

Scholar D. L. Ashliman connected changeling myths directly to harsh subsistence struggles across pre-industrial Europe. Peasant households depended upon every healthy family member sharing demanding farm labor. Stories of insatiable changelings mirrored real heartbreak when families faced illness and scarcity.

Medieval Scandinavian legends portrayed trolls eager for respectable human upbringings, often targeting unbaptised infants. Because folklore claimed trolls feared iron, Nordic parents balanced sharp iron tools atop cradles. Scottish ballads meanwhile linked changelings to mysterious birth cauls and fairy debts.

A beloved Swedish folk tale contrasted cruel superstitions with compassionate maternal love toward an innocent child. Refusing to mistreat the troll child in her care, the mother won her lost son back. Author Helena Nyblom immortalized Swedish troll folklore in classic children's literature.

pages.text: Recurring throughout European folklore, the changeling signified a supernatural substitute allegedly left when fairies or trolls abducted human offspring. A1-A2.headline: How Anti-War Movements Protest Armed Conflict Worldwide

pages.text: An anti-war movement is a public social movement opposing a nation's decision to begin or continue an armed conflict. Protesters rally against weapons fairs and fighting, ranging from strict pacifism opposing all force to objections against one specific war.

pages.text: During the American Civil War, opposition to fighting reached national politics when Peace Democrat George B. McClellan ran against President Abraham Lincoln. Fierce protests also erupted in the New York Draft Riots, where rioters attacked troops over unfair military conscription rules.

When World War One approached, British military camps felt war looming before mechanized battlefields horrified all of Europe. Shocked by modern industrial violence, European artists and writers in avant-garde movements like Dada turned openly anti-war.

Organized opposition to the Vietnam War started quietly on American college campuses before growing into massive national coalitions as casualties rose. Meanwhile in Vietnam, peace activist Ngo Ba Thanh joined global women's peace groups demanding peace and human rights.

pages.text: Early planning began when India's Department of Telecommunications finalized system requirements through the Telecommunication Engineering Center alongside security agencies. Legally, telephone interception orders in India draw authority from rules created under the historic Indian Telegraph Act. Those national telegraph rules specify which senior government authorities may issue official message interception directions.

A1-A2.headline: Antibiotics on Farms and Human Health

pages.text: Farmers give antibiotics to livestock animals to cure illness and prevent sudden farm disease outbreaks. Public health warnings explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria can spread easily from farm animals into people. Worldwide, farm animals consume more antimicrobials than human patients do.

pages.text: Rising antibiotic resistance threatens both human hospital care and farm animal welfare in future decades. Overusing medicines on crowded farms lets tough antibiotic-resistant bacteria enter soil, water, and food. Protecting antibiotics keeps life-saving drugs working safely.

Since early modern decades, antibiotics changed farming, fishing fleets, and commercial food plants around the world. After American meat shortages, farms expanded rapidly using low-dose drugs to help animals grow faster. Soon global meat production depended heavily on routine farm antibiotics.

Almost every country regulates livestock drugs today, often letting only trained veterinarians prescribe strong farm antibiotics. Health rules stop harmful antibiotic leftovers from hiding inside meat, milk, eggs, and honey. Careful laws vary widely across nations and continents.

Following early American meat shortages, crowded livestock facilities discovered low antibiotic doses sped animal growth. Rapid productivity gains entrenched routine agricultural dosing worldwide.

Economic pressures subsequently normalized widespread feed medication across farming systems.

A1-A2.headline: Waves of Change: Inside the Global Feminist Movement

pages.text: The feminist movement—often called the women's movement—is a broad series of social and political campaigns working to end unfair inequality between men and women. Across Western history, scholars often describe its modern journey through four major waves advocating women's rights and liberation.
pages.caption: The "We Can Do It!" war-propaganda poster from 1943 was re-appropriated as a symbol of the feminist movement in the 1980s.

evidence.fileTitle: File:We Can Do It! NARA 535413 - Restoration 2.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The "We Can Do It!" war-propaganda poster from 1943 was re-appropriated as a symbol of the feminist movement in the 1980s.

pages.text: Throughout history, unequal patriarchal systems sparked resistance from women fighting for fairness long before modern politics. In North America, Haudenosaunee nations practiced gender equality traditions well before European colonization, while early American activists organized alongside abolition and suffrage campaigns.

Activist Elizabeth Cady Stanton looked back proudly on the historic Seneca Falls Convention as the very first women's rights convention held in the world. Participants read and signed a bold declaration calling for equal civic dignity.
No single date marks when feminist thinking first began, because thoughtful women have written about equality and dignity for thousands of years across diverse civilizations around the world.

Beyond laws and voting rights, feminists have also reshaped everyday language to feel fairer and more welcoming. Many promote neutral titles like Ms for both married and unmarried women and inclusive words such as humanity.

B1-B2.headline: From Seneca Falls to Modern Waves: The Feminist Movement

pages.text: Grounded in challenging centuries of patriarchal authority, women's organizing predated formal political parties. Long before European colonization, Haudenosaunee nations maintained strong traditions of gender equality, while early American protofeminists mobilized through abolitionist and suffrage networks.

Reflecting years later, pioneer Elizabeth Cady Stanton hailed the Seneca Falls Convention as the world's first dedicated women's rights convention. Delegates debated and signed a landmark declaration demanding equal legal and social standing.

Historians emphasize that the feminist movement has been an ongoing social force across civilizations, making it impossible to determine an exact founding date. Women across many cultures have been writing thoughtfully about equality and dignity for thousands of years.

Cultural reform has extended directly into everyday speech and writing as well. Many feminists champion non-sexist and gender-inclusive language—favoring the title Ms regardless of marital status and using terms like humanity instead of male-centered defaults.

pages.text: The feminist movement—synonymous with the women's movement—unites sustained social mobilizations and political campaigns challenging institutionalized gender inequality. Within Western historiography, its trajectory is commonly periodized into four distinct waves progressing from middle-class suffrage advocacy toward intersectional liberation.

pages.text: Rooted in contesting deeply entrenched patriarchal hierarchies, organized advocacy drew upon varied historical precedents. Haudenosaunee societies practiced structured gender equality prior to European colonization, while early American protofeminists forged organizing strategies within abolitionist and suffrage coalitions.

In a retrospective address, Elizabeth Cady Stanton characterized the Seneca Falls Convention as humanity's inaugural women's rights convention, where attendees formally read and subscribed to a foundational declaration of equal rights.

Because women across diverse civilizations have authored incisive egalitarian critiques across millennia of recorded history, scholars stress that the feminist movement functions as an enduring historical force that resists reduction to any single founding date or location.

Alongside legal and political milestones, feminist advocacy has actively reshaped linguistic norms. Proponents encourage non-sexist and gender-inclusive phrasing—popularizing marital-status-neutral honorifics such as Ms and replacing generic masculine terms with inclusive equivalents like humanity.
